newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica maize harvest still slow despite dry spell.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica maize harvest still slow despite dry spell.

text.p: Harvesting of the 1997 South African crop is still proceeding very slowly despite the return of dry weather after unseasonal rains in late May, the National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo) said on Wednesday.
"It has been drier but it has also been abnormally cold, so cereals are not drying off as fast as they would normally do," said Kit le Clus, Nampo research and development director.
"They are harvesting patches on the high ground here and there, but overall it is very, very slow."
Harvest prospects were brightest on sandier soils, particularly in the west, where white maize dominates and the rains had not been so heavy.

Forecasters predict continued dry weather through the weekend. But le Klus said the eastern Free State would not be able to bring in the bulk of the crop for several weeks, pointing to a much slower yellow maize harvest.
The harvest delays have pushed up old crop prices as local millers and shippers scramble for scant supplies.

South Africa's 1997 commercial maize harvest was officially estimated at 7.66 million tonnes by the National Crop Estimates committee last month, down from last year's bumper production of 9.69 million.
A 7.66-million-tonne crop should leave over one million tonnes for export after allowing for average consumption of between 6.0-6.5 million tonnes.
This year's crop is expected to deliver 4.109 million tonnes of white maize and 3.551 million tonnes of yellow, compared to 1996's 5.836 million of white and 3.858 million of yellow.

The current season is the first year of full deregulation. The state Maize Board is currently being wound up and since the start of the new season on May 1, private traders have been free to export as much maize as they want.
